analysis.one_liner: Gives a federal tax credit for donations that pay private school scholarships for families.
analysis.headline: Rep. Adrian Smith introduced the bill on January 28, 2025 with 27 Republican cosponsors; it was referred to two House committees and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new federal tax credit, worth up to $5,000 or 10% of a donor's income per year, for people who give money to nonprofit scholarship groups. Those groups hand out scholarships to students from households earning up to 300% of their area's median income, and the money can pay for private or religious school tuition, tutoring, homeschooling materials, and therapies for students with disabilities. The program is capped at $5 billion per year from 2025 through 2028, and it bars federal, state, and local governments from restricting how the money is used at private or religious schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Families below 300% of area median income who want private, religious, or homeschool options for their children — the scholarships can cover tuition, tutoring, testing fees, dual college enrollment, and therapies for disabled students, and the scholarships themselves are tax-free. Donors get a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit, which is worth the most to households with large tax bills. Private and religious schools gain a new stream of tuition revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families using private or religious schools

how_it_helps.text: The credit equals a donor's qualified contributions, up to the greater of $5,000 or 10% of adjusted gross income per year, with unused credit carried forward up to five years.

Scholarships go to students in households with income at or below 300% of the area median, and cover private, religious, and homeschool expenses including tuition, tutoring, standardized tests, dual enrollment, and educational therapies.
Scholarship money received by families is excluded from gross income, so it is not taxed.
10% of the annual $5 billion cap is divided evenly among the states, and a real-time tracking system shows donors when the cap is used up.
The bill prohibits federal, state, and local governments from imposing requirements that block or discourage the use of scholarship funds at private or religious schools.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through forgone revenue of up to $5 billion per year for four years. Public school systems may also bear a cost if students leave with scholarship money and per-pupil funding follows them out the door. The bill does not identify an offsetting source of revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and public school budgets

drawbacks.text: The program costs the Treasury up to $5 billion per year for 2025 through 2028, allocated first-come first-serve, with no designated pay-for.

Because a dollar-for-dollar credit is only useful to someone who owes federal tax (or can wait out a five-year carryforward), the largest tax benefit goes to higher-income donors, and the income ceiling for students — 300% of area median income — is far above a typical family's earnings.
Scholarship groups may keep up to 10% of receipts for administration, and organizations may carry over 15% of receipts to the next year.

The bill overrides state and local rules that would restrict scholarship use at private or religious schools, which supporters call protecting parental choice and critics call tying the hands of state governments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family that gets a scholarship, the help is real: tax-free money for tuition, tutoring, or therapies they otherwise could not afford. But the financing mechanism is generous to donors regardless of how the money is used, and the student income ceiling reaches deep into upper-middle incomes, so a large share of the $5 billion in annual tax value is expected to flow to households that were already paying private school tuition or already donating — a subsidy for a choice they had made anyway. Meanwhile the cost lands on general revenue and, indirectly, on public school systems that lose per-pupil funding when students leave. A better-targeted design would lower the income ceiling and raise the bar for what donors capture.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 28, 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce committees, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith of Nebraska introduced the bill on January 28, 2025.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action — no committee vote, hearing, or floor consideration — appears in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet, because nothing has happened beyond the referral. If the bill dies, public school budgets and federal revenue are preserved; if it advances, private schools and high-income donors gain the most.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 27 cosponsors from his party.

for.name: 27 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred yet; the sponsor and all 27 cosponsors are Republicans, and the bill awaits action in two House committees.

industries.note: Credit-funded scholarships create a new tuition revenue stream flowing to private and religious schools, and the bill bars governments from conditioning that money on school policies, including religious ones. Families who use the schools gain access, while public schools lose students and funding.

The bill creates a class of 501(c)(3) intermediaries that collect credit-backed donations and distribute scholarships, and may keep up to 10% of receipts for administration. They must undergo annual independent audits and verify student income.

A dollar-for-dollar credit worth up to 10% of adjusted gross income is most valuable to households with the largest tax bills, and unused credit can be carried forward five years. The cost of that offset is forgone federal revenue borne by all taxpayers.

Every scholarship used to leave a public school takes that student's state and local per-pupil funding with them, while the federal credit gives nothing back to the district. Families who leave gain options; the districts and remaining students absorb the loss.

industries.industry: Tutoring, online education, and therapy providers
industries.note: Qualified expenses include tutoring by licensed instructors, online educational materials, and occupational, behavioral, physical, and speech therapies for students with disabilities, creating new paying customers in those fields.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been dormant in committee since its referral in January 2025. A nearly identical federal scholarship tax credit was included in the major tax and spending package signed into law in July 2025 (widely reported), which greatly reduces the odds this standalone bill advances on its own; it will most likely remain pending or die quietly unless its provisions are needed again in a future tax package.
